brief: Global bond selloff: 10Y Treasuries had their worst session since Liberation Day (April last year), 5Y yields topped 5% for the first time since 2007, and 10Y yields widened another 8bps the next day. Brent is up ~73% in 2026 and CPI has risen from 2.4% in January to an expected 3.60% in September, but the author argues this is not an inflation scare: of the ~97bps YTD rise in 10Y nominal yields, only ~10bps came from breakevens, which have been stable for three years, while the rest is real yields at 2008 levels; term premium has stayed range-bound, ruling out fiscal fears. The move is instead read as policy rates and a higher neutral rate, driven by economic strength (Atlanta Fed GDPNow at 5.08%, Q3 S&P 500 earnings growth ~30%) and competition for capital, which the author frames as AI capex via hyperscaler bond issuance (Goldman: $420bn+ next year, ~60% of 2027 Treasury DV01 issuance). Raskin argues the neutral rate now sits near the upper bound of its plausible range.
